hero.subtitle: Saint-Moré, Yonne — Burgundy, France
hero.title: Camp de Cora
hero.tagline: Two thousand years of memory in the heart of Burgundy

home.intro_text: Overlooking the Cure Valley, the Camp de Cora spans more than 20 hectares of Burgundian forest. Here, people succeeded one another for six millennia — Neolithic settlers, Bronze Age warriors, Gauls, Roman legionnaires, Merovingians. Their traces are still here, carved in stone and earth.
home.highlight_roman_text: Established on the Via Agrippa in the 1st century, guarding the Lyon-Boulogne road
home.highlight_monument_text: Listed since 1971 — 300m wall, 6 towers, defensive moat
home.highlight_prehistory_text: From the Neolithic to the Merovingians, an exceptional site in Burgundy
home.saint_more_title: Saint-Moré, a village in the heart of Yonne
home.saint_more_text: Nestled in the Cure Valley, 29 km from Auxerre, the village of Saint-Moré (89270) takes its name from the ancient site of Cora. Its 176 inhabitants live at the foot of an exceptional heritage, a few kilometres from the famous Arcy-sur-Cure caves and 13 km from the Basilica of Vézelay, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

history.title: The History of Cora
history.subtitle: From prehistory to the dawn of the Middle Ages
history.period_neolithic_text: Six thousand years ago, people chose this limestone promontory to settle. The location was ideal: commanding the Cure Valley, defensible on three sides, close to water. Excavations have uncovered incised pottery, knapped flint tools, millstones and loom weights. Two successive phases of occupation correspond to the Burgundian and Chasséen cultures — evidence of a dense and lasting settlement from the Neolithic onwards.
history.period_bronze_text: Around 950 BC, the site undergoes a new impulse. Mastery of bronze transforms social organisation: weapons, tools and ornaments attest to a hierarchical community. The promontory is fortified. Animal bones — cattle, pigs, sheep — confirm a structured agro-pastoral economy. Saint-Moré becomes a power hub in the Cure Valley.
history.period_iron_text: In the Iron Age, the site asserts itself as a Gaulish oppidum, probably held by the Aedui or Lingones — two Gaulish peoples competing for control of this strategic zone between the Saône and Loire rivers. The position dominates the natural passage of the Cure Valley, an essential communication axis. When Rome extended its hold over Gaul after 52 BC, the promontory of Cora entered the orbit of Roman civilisation.
history.period_roman_text: Under Augustus, Marcus Agrippa — the emperor's son-in-law and general — was tasked with criss-crossing Gaul with a network of roads and military camps. The Via Agrippa, linking Lugdunum (Lyon) to Gesoriacum (Boulogne-sur-Mer), followed the Cure Valley. The promontory of Cora became a castrum: a 300-metre wall built in Roman masonry, 6 to 7 cylindrical flanking towers, a 150-metre moat hewn from the rock. The garrison protected convoys, monitored movements and maintained order in this wooded, enclosed valley prone to ambushes. Coins found span from Nero (1st century) to Valentinian II (4th century) — over three centuries of continuous military occupation.
history.period_merovingian_text: The fall of the Western Roman Empire (476 AD) did not mean the abandonment of the site. Under the Merovingians, inhabitants continued to occupy the promontory and its surroundings. The most striking evidence: sarcophagi were carved directly into the nearby limestone cliff, using the rock as raw material. These tombs from the 6th to 8th century bear witness to real Christianisation and a living community — six millennia after the first Neolithic settlers.
history.period_discovery_text: It was in the 19th century that Camp de Cora regained scholarly notoriety. Abbé Poulaine conducted the first methodical excavations, unearthing iron weapons, silver medals and imperial coins. In 1852, Baudoin and Marcel Bonneville carried out more systematic digs: 592 ceramic vases, 379 flint flakes, 19 bronze objects, 10 millstones, and Gaulish coins of the Lingones and Aedui. Abbé Parat completed this documentation, laying the foundations of modern knowledge of the site. Listed as a Historic Monument on 14 September 1971, Camp de Cora officially joined the national heritage.
history.via_agrippa_title: The Via Agrippa — Backbone of Roman Gaul
history.via_agrippa_text: Commissioned by Marcus Agrippa around 20 BC, the Via Agrippa of the Ocean linked Lugdunum (Lyon) to Gesoriacum (Boulogne-sur-Mer) over more than 900 kilometres. Paved with limestone slabs, 4 to 6 metres wide, marked with milestones, it was the backbone of the Roman communication network in Gaul. Camp de Cora was one of its key control points: first to protect construction crews in this enclosed valley, then to permanently secure this vital axis between the Mediterranean and the Channel.

site.title: The Site Today
site.subtitle: Listed Historic Monument since 1971
site.wall_text: The main rampart of Camp de Cora extends 190 to 300 metres depending on which sections are still standing. 2.70 metres thick, built in careful Roman masonry alternating limestone rubble and brick courses, it originally rose to 3 to 7 metres in height. Six to seven cylindrical flanking towers — spaced at regular intervals — allowed defenders to enfilade attackers advancing along the wall. Despite twenty centuries of abandonment and stone robbing for local buildings, significant sections still stand — a remarkably rare feat for a Gallo-Roman fortification of this period.
site.moat_text: In front of the rampart, a monumental moat reinforces the defensive system: 150 metres long, 12 to 18 metres wide, 2 to 2.5 metres deep, partly cut into the limestone. This moat was the first obstacle for any attacker. Its V or U profile, characteristic of Roman military architecture, is still perfectly legible today despite partial silting over the centuries. The CORA2025 topographic survey, carried out with a Leica total station in May 2025, provided the most accurate digital mapping of it to date.
site.classification_text: On 14 September 1971, the rampart and remains of Camp de Cora were officially inscribed in the French Historic Monuments register under reference PA00113833. This legal protection, granted by the Ministry of Culture, prohibits any unauthorised modification, demolition or excavation, and opens the right to grants for restoration. An indispensable recognition to ensure the survival of this exceptional heritage against the pressures of time and vegetation.
site.restoration_text: Maintaining a listed monument deep in the forest is a permanent battle against encroaching vegetation. Every summer for several years, the Association Cora Patrimoine and Union Rempart have organised 15-day volunteer worksites: clearing the top and faces of the rampart, sorting and repositioning fallen stones, repointing with traditional air lime mortar — the only binder compatible with Roman masonry. In May 2025, a complete topographic survey was carried out with a Leica total station, producing a precise digital plan (DXF) that will serve as the basis for the next restoration phases.

itineraries.title: Visit & Explore
itineraries.subtitle: 3 itineraries to discover the site and its surroundings
itineraries.access_text: The Camp de Cora is located 1 km south of the village of Saint-Moré (89270), on a rocky promontory overlooking the Cure river. Departure from the parking near the church, with information panels.
itineraries.access_car: By car: from the A6 motorway, exit Nitry or Avallon, then D100 towards Saint-Moré. Free parking in the village.
itineraries.access_train: By train: Avallon station (25 km) or Auxerre (35 km), then taxi or bicycle.
itineraries.route1_desc: The main circuit. From the village, climb to the camp, visit the rampart and towers, descend to the prehistoric caves of Saint-Moré.
itineraries.route2_desc: Discovery of Merovingian sarcophagi carved into the limestone cliff. A striking testament to the continuity of occupation after the fall of Rome.
itineraries.route3_desc: Forest walk to the miraculous fountain of Saint-Moré. Shaded path, ideal for families.

association.title: Association Cora Patrimoine
association.subtitle: Preserve, restore, pass on
association.mission_text: The Association Cora Patrimoine has been working for several years to protect and promote the Camp de Cora. In partnership with Union Rempart — a network of 180 heritage associations in France — we organise volunteer restoration worksites every summer.
association.work_item2: Consolidating stones with traditional lime mortar
association.join_text: Join us! Your membership directly supports the preservation of this exceptional heritage. As a member, you receive our newsletters, are invited to our events, and participate in the life of the association.
